prompt: A production inference endpoint changed after the champion alias moved. The canary was HTTP-ready, aggregate accuracy improved from 91.0% to 91.4%, p50 latency stayed flat and GPU allocation showed one device per Pod. Complaint rate doubled for one language, p99 time to first token tripled, two Pods restarted with GPU out-of-memory, and cost per completed task rose 70%. Explain the first safe response and the evidence needed before promotion or rollback.
directAnswer: Stop further exposure, preserve request and release lineage, route affected traffic to the last known compatible immutable release when the rollback path is proven, and investigate quality, latency, memory and cost by cohort. The alias, readiness, aggregate score and allocated-GPU count are not sufficient deployment evidence.
foundation: A model endpoint is a distributed production release, not a file behind an HTTP port. The deployed identity includes data, feature code, model and tokenizer digests, prompt, retrieval and policy versions, image digest, runtime and route. HTTP readiness says a process can receive traffic. It does not say answers are acceptable, deadlines are met, GPU memory fits peaks or the result is economical.
reasoningSteps: Freeze alias and traffic mutations so the evidence does not continue changing.
Resolve each served request to immutable release, model, tokenizer, prompt, policy, image and runtime identities rather than the champion label.
Protect users by stopping the ramp and shifting only through a tested route to the previous compatible warm release; verify postconditions.
Slice quality and complaint outcomes by language, tenant, operation, request length, release and time instead of relying on aggregate accuracy.
Decompose latency into gateway, queue, prefill, time to first token, decode or time per output token, post-processing and total duration.
Bind out-of-memory events to device profile, weights, runtime workspace, KV cache, batch and concurrency peaks; allocation is not memory capacity.
Calculate completed useful outcomes, tokens, GPU-seconds and cost by release so throughput gains cannot hide lower value.
Find the first failed gate, correct the release or platform contract, rerun offline and representative canary evidence, and only then consider promotion.
seniorAnswer: I would declare a release-quality incident and stop the canary ramp. First I would pin the actual immutable release behind every route and preserve alias history, deployment receipts and request IDs. I would restore the last compatible release through the rehearsed rollback path if paired user evidence shows material harm. Then I would compare the same representative cohorts by language, request length and tenant across release versions. I would inspect success and quality outcomes alongside queue age, TTFT, TPOT, token counts, GPU memory components, restarts and cost per useful completion. The likely failure is not one metric: an aggregate evaluation gate hid a critical slice, the latency gate ignored tail and stage timing, GPU admission counted devices rather than memory demand, and the promotion gate omitted unit economics. Prevention is an immutable release manifest, sliced evaluation, per-release telemetry, memory admission, progressive exposure with minimum samples, and a warm compatible rollback target.
weakAnswer: The model has higher accuracy and the Pods are ready, so add more GPU replicas and wait for the canary to stabilize.
whyWeak: It treats aggregate offline quality as user benefit, readiness as correctness, and device count as usable memory. Adding identical replicas can repeat OOM, does not repair a harmed language cohort, and changes the evidence during an unsafe rollout.

evidence.signal: Immutable release manifest and alias audit
evidence.proves: Which artifact set was approved, routed and mutable-pointer changes made

evidence.signal: Per-release sliced quality and complaint outcomes
evidence.doesNotProve: Causality without allocation and confounder checks

evidence.signal: Queue, TTFT, TPOT, token and end-to-end distributions
GPU memory component peaks and OOM events
evidence.proves: Whether admitted weights, cache, workspace and batches fit observed devices
evidence.doesNotProve: Future capacity under a different workload

evidence.proves: Observed resource economics connected to an outcome definition

followUps.prompt: Why is a registry alias unsafe as the only deployment identity?
followUps.answer: An alias is a mutable pointer. It can resolve to a different immutable version later, while caches and replicas may refresh at different times. Record both the alias decision and the resolved version and digest in the release and request evidence.

followUps.prompt: Why can p50 remain healthy while users suffer?
followUps.answer: The median hides tail cohorts and stage-specific waiting. A small population can wait in queue, suffer long prefill or decode slowly while at least half of requests remain fast.

followUps.prompt: Should every detected drift retrain automatically?
followUps.answer: No. Telemetry changes, schema breakage, population mix, delayed labels, serving bugs and cost shifts can look like drift. Classify and validate the change before authorizing a versioned candidate and promotion.
